In Pakistan today, career expectations and reality couldn't be further apart.
Thousands of students rush into trending degrees driven by hype — entering with sky-high expectations, but zero practical guidance.

The result? Students spend years and thousands of rupees on a degree, only to realize halfway through that the field wasn't meant for them, or that the job market looks nothing like what was promised.

To fix this, I built Career OS for the Alibaba Group, Alibaba Cloud AI Hackathon Pakistan 2026.

Career OS is an AI-powered platform that guides students from choosing the right degree and finding scholarships to landing their first job — backed by verified local data, real PKR salary realities, and hands-on preparation.

Under the hood:
⚡ 1. Alibaba Cloud DashScope, Qwen & Qoder
Powered by Qwen (qwen-plus-2025-07-28) with automated fallbacks (qwen-plus → qwen-vl-thinking → qwen-turbo) to ensure uptime while enforcing strict Pydantic JSON contracts.

🛡️ 2. MCP Grounding over SSE
Instead of guessing from memory, the AI connects to Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool servers over SSE (MCP/career_server, MCP/pke_server). It fetches verified records first, giving students accurate facts without hallucinations.

📊 3. The Pakistan Knowledge Engine (PKE)
A structured data layer cataloging:
🔹 248 recognized universities & 210 degree programs
🔹Localized career pathways & industry skill maps
🔹 Real PKR-based entry and mid-level salary ranges
🔹 Scholarships, provincial quotas, and merit criteria

🎯 4. Real Momentum, Not Static Advice
🔹 7-Day Career Trials: "Test-drive" a profession through hands-on tasks before spending 4 years on a degree.
🔹 Next Best Action (NBA) Engine: Prescribes the exact practical step to take next.
🔹 AI Mock Interviews: Job interview simulations scored from 0 to 10 (MCQs based) to prepare students for real hiring.

🛠️ The Tech Stack:
🔹 Next.js 14, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion
🔹 FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, SQLite (WAL) / PostgreSQL
🔹 DashScope Qwen, MCP over SSE, Pydantic (800+ tests)
🔹 Deployment: Vercel + Render / Docker

Washington spent this month arguing about AI safety without deciding much, and the part I keep thinking about is not how loud the argument got but where the actual leverage sits.

Two bills are on the table. The FRONTIER Act from Obernolte and Trahan scales requirements by company size. The Thune, Klobuchar and Cruz proposal would let companies test their own models for catastrophic risk and report what they find. Speaker Johnson says he wants the labs in a room by winter to work out some consensus on guardrails. The administration's new review framework for advanced models leaves out public incident reporting, and Trump is set to discuss AI safety with Xi at the end of the month.

Strip the names out and one question is left. When something goes wrong, who has to say so, and does anyone outside the company ever see it?

Self-testing is not automatically a dodge. The frontier labs have the best evaluation teams on the planet right now, and nobody in a Senate office is going to red team a frontier model. But a test you grade yourself and file privately is a different object from an incident you are required to disclose. The EU already mandates reporting for powerful models. We are still debating whether to ask nicely.

The size tiering bothers me for a reason closer to home. I build on top of these models. So do most of the founders in my feed. A rule tiered by company size puts a company like mine in the light touch tier, which is convenient and also where I think a lot of the real damage is going to surface. Not a rogue model escaping a lab. A wellness app saying something to a sixteen year old that no clinician ever reviewed. A hiring tool quietly sorting resumes on a proxy nobody audited. An agent with a billing API and sloppy permissions. The frontier lab has a hundred people on safety. The startup shipping on its API has a founder who skimmed the docs at midnight.

The other thread worth watching is red lines. Anthropic and the Defense Department went back and forth this year over contract language on autonomous weapons and mass surveillance, employees at Google and OpenAI pushed back publicly, and Schiff now has a bill to write those limits into law. That fight is clarifying because it forces an answer about a specific system and a specific use, allowed or not, rather than another round of how much oversight in general.

A former Anthropic researcher's warning pulled over 150 million views this summer. That is not a policy victory. It tells you a lot of people are uneasy and have nowhere to put it, and uneasiness with no channel tends to produce either bad law or no law at all.

So if you are building something, do not wait to find out which tier you land in. Write down what your system must never do. Decide who gets told when it does it anyway. Keep the log somewhere you would not mind a regulator reading. It costs almost nothing now and it is expensive to retrofit later.

A strong product does not automatically create a strong APAC business.

This is particularly true for AI-native enterprise software.

APAC is often discussed as one region, but selling across Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines and Greater China requires very different approaches to trust, buying committees, partnerships, implementation and executive engagement.

Through my years of building technology businesses and leading enterprise sales across Asia Pacific, I have learnt that sustainable regional growth depends on five disciplines:

(1) Localise the go-to-market motion—not merely the product.
The business problem, buyer priorities and decision process can differ substantially across markets.

(2) Establish the right enterprise use cases.
AI attracts attention, but measurable business outcomes secure commitment. Customers need to understand what will improve, how it will be measured and when value will be realised. The real value to clients is how exactly can the offering be designed and deployed for optimised utilisation, not just merely a tool, or a great tool.

(3) Treat partners as an extension of the business.
A partner logo does not create a channel. Partners require enablement, opportunity alignment, joint accountability and a commercially compelling reason to invest.

(4) Build customer success into the sales strategy.
Winning the contract is only the beginning. Adoption, utilisation and measurable value determine renewal, expansion and long-term credibility.

(5) Introduce operating discipline early.
Clear qualification, realistic forecasting, defined sales stages and consistent leadership reviews are essential before regional complexity begins to scale. Core Sales DNA & fundamentals will be key.

APAC growth is therefore not simply about hiring more salespeople.

It is about building a methodical, repeatable commercial system & workflow that brings together product, people, partners and customer outcomes—while respecting the realities of each market.

The companies that understand this will not merely enter APAC.
They will earn the right to grow here.

Melbourne Procurement: A Market Split Four Ways
  
Right now, there's no shortage of good procurement people in Melbourne,  redundancies have widened the pool considerably. But "plenty of talent available" hides a much messier reality underneath it, because the market isn't treating everyone in that pool the same way.
  
At one end, the strongest contractors I speak with are still moving fast, picked up almost as quickly as they surface. Just below them, solid, genuinely experienced professionals are finding it far more competitive than they're used to; good CVs sitting in inboxes for longer than they would have twelve months ago.
  
Then there's a group I think gets overlooked in most of these market updates: people who've spent years at CPO, Head of Procurement or genuine executive level. There simply aren't enough roles at that altitude to go around. And stepping down into a hands-on contract isn't the easy landing it sounds like, plenty are being told, politely, that they're now too senior for the work. Twenty years of strong procurement experience, genuinely available, and no obvious seat in the current market that fits where their career has actually landed.
  
The permanent hiring process is where most of the frustration is coming from. AI screening, psychometrics, panel interviews, stakeholder interviews,  one client recently described a process with six separate interview stages!  I understand the instinct to de-risk a senior appointment, but at some point the process stops protecting the decision and starts becoming the obstacle to it. These are people who've spent their careers hiring others, managing teams, negotiating hard commercial outcomes, and several have told me, plainly, that the process itself is what's wearing them down.
  
Contracting is moving at a completely different pace. Most of the assignments I'm working right now have a hiring cycle of around two weeks, which tracks, given the ask is usually someone walking in and delivering something specific over three or six months.
  
So, the honest picture of Melbourne procurement isn't one market, it's four running at once: a deeper talent pool overall, top contractors still moving quickly, strong professionals facing real competition for the first time in years, and senior leaders finding fewer seats than their experience would suggest. Where you sit in that mix determines whether this feels like a tight market or a slow one, and right now, those experiences barely resemble each other.

2026 is the year Agentic AI stops being a lab experiment and becomes a production reality. The shift is not about building smarter chatbots or autoregressive loops. It is about designing systems that can plan, execute, and adapt without human hand-holding.

Three technical observations from the front lines of building multi-agent systems right now.

First, multi-agent orchestration is becoming the "microservices moment" for AI. Just as you would not build a monolithic application in 2022, you should not build a monolithic agent in 2026. Breaking an agent into specialized sub-agents for perception, reasoning, and action creates fault isolation and composability. The hardest lesson is that coordination overhead grows quadratically with agent count. The winning architectures use a lightweight orchestrator that delegates to narrowly-scoped workers, then evaluates outcomes before routing to the next step.

Second, protocol standardization is quietly creating an "Agent Internet." The MCP (Model Context Protocol) and A2A (Agent-to-Agent) protocols are removing the friction of agents talking to each other across boundaries. This is not just about API compatibility. It is about establishing a shared contract for state, intent, and rollback. An agent that fails mid-task must be able to signal its failure state to the orchestrator, not just crash silently. Teams that adopt these protocols early are seeing 40 percent faster integration times with external systems.

Third, healthcare is the unexpected proving ground for agentic decision-making. Agents are moving from pattern recognition to active involvement in diagnosis and treatment planning. The critical insight is that autonomy requires asymmetrical trust. The agent can propose a treatment plan, but the human must be able to inspect the reasoning chain and override it. Building that fallback logic is not a feature. It is the core safety infrastructure.

You don't need to hire an SDR to get SDR outcomes.

Hiring is the default move, but it's expensive, slow (60 to 90 days to ramp), and risky if your ICP or messaging isn't dialed in yet. Before you post that job, here's what I'd try first:

1. Fractional or contract SDR services Agencies and fractional SDR providers can run a proven outbound motion for you for a fraction of the fully loaded cost of a hire, and you can turn it off if it's not working. No severance, no awkward conversation.

2. AI assisted outbound tooling Tools that handle research, enrichment, and first draft personalization (Clay plus an AI writing layer, for example) let a founder or AE run outbound in 30 to 60 minutes a day instead of needing a full time researcher or writer.

3. Founder led outbound, systemized The founder doing 20 highly targeted, well researched outbound touches a week, using the signal based approach, often outperforms a green SDR doing 200 generic touches. Quality over volume, especially pre PMF.

4. Automate the qualification, not the relationship Chatbots and intake forms can pre qualify inbound leads (budget, timeline, use case) before a human ever gets involved. This replicates the "qualify" part of the SDR role without a headcount.

When you should actually hire:

You have a repeatable, documented outbound playbook that's already working
You have more qualified opportunity volume than your AEs can handle
You've validated messaging and ICP well enough that a new hire has a real script to follow, not a blank page

Hiring an SDR to find your playbook is expensive trial and error. Hiring an SDR to scale a playbook that already works is leverage.

Get the outcome first. Hire to scale it, not to discover it.
